title: 2 Things You Didn't Know About the McLaren F1

scenes.text: The McLaren F one was built with a small amount of real gold inside its engine bay. Not as decoration. As a heat shield. And the same car, a road car with a luggage set and air conditioning, went on to win the twenty-four hours of Le Mans at its very first attempt, even though its creator never wanted it to race. Those are the two things you probably did not know about the McLaren F one.
scenes.caption: 2 THINGS YOU DIDN'T KNOW ABOUT THE McLAREN F1

scenes.text: Here is the twist. The first fact explains why the second one was possible. Because the same obsession that led to gold foil, an obsession with weight and heat, is what made a road car light enough and reliable enough to beat purpose-built prototypes in the rain.
scenes.caption: THE GOLD AND THE RACE ARE CONNECTED

scenes.text: Every figure in this video comes from a published source, listed in the description. Where a number is an estimate, or our own arithmetic, we will say so. Let's start with the gold.
scenes.caption: EVERY FIGURE IS SOURCED

scenes.text: Wikipedia says that to protect the car from the heat of its own engine, the designers lined the engine bay with a highly efficient heat reflector, gold foil. The page adds a precise number. Approximately sixteen grams, about half an ounce, of gold was used in each car.
scenes.query: McLaren F1 gold foil engine bay
scenes.caption: ~16 GRAMS OF GOLD IN EVERY CAR

scenes.text: Why gold? Because it reflects heat extremely well. And the F one needed that, because of where the engine sits. Another source, the Gooding and Company auction coverage, explains that gold foil was used in specific areas to reduce heat transfer, an important consideration in a car where the V twelve sat just behind the cabin.
scenes.caption: GOLD REFLECTS HEAT

scenes.text: That engine matters too. Wikipedia says it was a BMW S seventy slash two, a sixty-degree V twelve of six thousand sixty-four cubic centimeters, designed by BMW's motorsport division under Paul Rosche. It made six hundred eighteen horsepower at seven thousand four hundred r p m, and four hundred seventy-nine pound-feet of torque at five thousand six hundred.
scenes.caption: BMW V12: 618 HP, 6.1 LITERS

scenes.text: The engine alone weighed two hundred sixty-six kilograms, or five hundred eighty-six pounds, according to Wikipedia. And it was not McLaren's first choice. Gooding and Company says that McLaren's Formula One cars used Honda engines in the late nineteen eighties, but Honda would not build an engine for the road car.
scenes.caption: HONDA SAID NO

scenes.text: So designer Gordon Murray shopped around, the article says, and found a collaborator in BMW's motorsport division. One of Murray's non-negotiables was that the engine had to be naturally aspirated, with no turbos. And the result made far more power than planned. The car's original goal was five hundred fifty horsepower. The engine delivered six hundred twenty-seven metric horsepower without further tuning.
scenes.caption: THE GOAL WAS 550 HP

scenes.text: Do the arithmetic. Six hundred eighteen horsepower against a goal of five hundred fifty is about twelve percent more than planned, by our own arithmetic. But the engine also came in above Murray's planned weight limit, Gooding and Company says. Even in the best car of its time, there were trade-offs.
scenes.caption: 12% MORE POWER THAN PLANNED

scenes.text: Gooding and Company adds that the engine drove the rear wheels only, through a transversely mounted six-speed manual gearbox. And Wikipedia gives the compression ratio, eleven to one. A naturally aspirated sixty-degree V twelve, with a manual gearbox, in a car that cost five hundred forty thousand pounds. No turbos, no paddles.
scenes.caption: NO TURBOS. NO PADDLES.

scenes.text: Now back to the gold. It was not the only precious thing in the car. Wikipedia says each F one came with a gold-plated Facom titanium tool kit and a first aid kit, both stored inside the car. A tool kit made of titanium and plated in gold, supplied with a road car.
scenes.caption: A GOLD-PLATED TITANIUM TOOL KIT

scenes.text: And there was luggage. Wikipedia says the car came with tailored, proprietary luggage bags specially designed to fit its carpeted storage compartments. Gooding and Company says the compartments sat above the rear wheel arches, and that the fitted luggage set was standard with every road car.
scenes.caption: FITTED LUGGAGE, STANDARD

scenes.text: So the F one was a car with a gold-lined engine bay, gold-plated tools and bespoke luggage. And yet it was also a car with no airbags, Wikipedia says. This was a machine built around weight, so every system that was not essential was left out, and every part that remained was made as light as possible.
scenes.caption: GOLD INSIDE, BUT NO AIRBAGS

scenes.text: The same obsession shows in the seating. Wikipedia says the driver's seat is positioned in the middle of the car, ahead of the fuel tank and ahead of the engine. Gooding and Company says it was a three-seat layout, with the driver front and centre, flanked by two passengers set slightly behind.
scenes.caption: DRIVER IN THE MIDDLE

scenes.text: And here is a detail many fans miss. Gooding and Company says Ferrari's Tre Posti three-seat three sixty-five P Berlinetta Speciale from nineteen sixty-six had used a similar layout, but that car was essentially a coachbuilt special, not a production car the way the F one would be. The idea was not new. Making it a production car was.
scenes.caption: A 1966 FERRARI HAD DONE IT FIRST

scenes.text: Wikipedia says Murray described his design concept as a common one among designers of high-performance cars: low weight and high power. He conceived the F one as an exercise in creating the ultimate road-going sports car. Low weight and high power. The gold foil was one small way of making that work.
scenes.caption: LOW WEIGHT, HIGH POWER

scenes.text: The numbers show how far that went. Wikipedia lists the F one at eleven hundred forty kilograms dry, or two thousand five hundred thirteen pounds, and twelve hundred sixty kilograms ready to drive. The SlashGear website points out that is just over twenty-five hundred pounds, lighter than a new Toyota Corolla at over twenty-nine hundred.
scenes.caption: 1,140 KG DRY

scenes.text: Now put the weight and the power together. Six hundred eighteen horsepower divided by eleven hundred forty kilograms is about point five four horsepower per kilogram, by our own arithmetic. That is the kind of ratio that, in the early nineteen nineties, almost nothing on the road could match.
scenes.caption: ~0.54 HP PER KILOGRAM

scenes.text: And there is one more story about this car's toughness, from the very beginning. Wikipedia reports that a test driver, wearing just shorts and a T-shirt, hit a rock and rolled the first prototype car several times. The car was built to a very high standard, and that incident showed what its carbon fiber body could take.
scenes.caption: THE PROTOTYPE THAT ROLLED

scenes.text: Gooding and Company says the F one was the first road car with a full carbon fiber chassis, with titanium, magnesium and Kevlar used in other areas to provide strength without adding weight. So the same materials that make the car light also protect the people inside it.
scenes.caption: FIRST ROAD CAR WITH A FULL CARBON CHASSIS

scenes.text: Wikipedia lists the tires, too. Two hundred thirty-five forty-five seventeen at the front, and three hundred fifteen forty-five seventeen at the rear. A rear tire three hundred fifteen millimeters wide is about twelve point four inches, by our own arithmetic. Wide rubber for a car with six hundred eighteen horsepower.
scenes.caption: 315 MM REAR TIRES

scenes.text: Murray also wanted carbon fiber brakes, Gooding and Company says, but the technology was still in its infancy. Here is the twist. The racing version, the GTR, did get carbon brakes, Wikipedia says. And Wikipedia's page on the nineteen ninety-five race says those lighter carbon brakes would not need changing through the entire race.
scenes.caption: CARBON BRAKES ARRIVED ON THE RACE CAR

scenes.text: The design of the body came from Peter Stevens, Gooding and Company says. It describes the exterior as simpler and more elegant than most other supercars of its era, with a shape not only dictated by aerodynamics. The car looked calm, even though it was extreme underneath.
scenes.caption: A CALM SHAPE, AN EXTREME CAR

scenes.text: That is thing number one. A car that spent gold on heat, and spent carbon fiber on weight, because every gram and every degree mattered. And that is exactly the reason it turned out to be better at racing than anybody expected, including the man who designed it.
scenes.caption: THING ONE: EVERY GRAM MATTERED

scenes.text: Now thing number two. Wikipedia's page on the F one GTR says Gordon Murray originally saw his creation as the ultimate road car, with no intention of racing it. Racing teams and private owners wanted a GT one car. And a Le Mans winner named John Nielsen turned to Murray, trying to convince him to offer factory backing.
scenes.caption: MURRAY DID NOT WANT TO RACE IT
scenes.chapter: Thing two: the race car nobody wanted

scenes.text: Motor Sport magazine tells a slightly different version. It says Ron Dennis, the head of McLaren, had an F one road car on order himself and wanted to go racing with it. Dennis asked his friend, racer Ray Bellm, for one million pounds to fund a one-off racing version. Bellm declined, and Dennis suggested he find other investors.
scenes.caption: DENNIS ASKED FOR £1 MILLION

scenes.text: Bellm went to Thomas Bscher, a German banker and historic racer, and brought in Lindsay Owen-Jones. Meanwhile, McLaren's composites department head, Jeff Hazell, had put together a proposal after a fact-finding trip to Le Mans in nineteen ninety-three. A more modest plan was approved after Hazell and Murray visited the May nineteen ninety-four Dijon round of what became the global endurance GT series.
scenes.caption: A FACT-FINDING TRIP TO DIJON

scenes.text: Eventually, Wikipedia says, Murray relented and agreed to modify the F one into a racing car. McLaren used an unused chassis, number nineteen, as a development prototype. The bodywork gained cooling ducts, a large central nose duct and a large adjustable rear wing.
scenes.caption: MURRAY RELENTED

scenes.text: The page says even the nineteen ninety-five version generated enough downforce to run along the ceiling at one hundred miles per hour. The interior was stripped of luxuries and given a full racing cage. Carbon brakes replaced the stock units. But the central seat, butterfly doors and standard gearbox stayed.
scenes.caption: DOWNFORCE TO DRIVE ON THE CEILING

scenes.text: The money was modest. Motor Sport says the initial development budget was seven hundred fifty thousand pounds, and a production run of five cars at six hundred twenty-five thousand pounds each funded the program. Customers included the Fayed family of Harrods and gentleman racer Jean-Luc Maury-Laribière. By comparison, the road car had launched at five hundred forty thousand pounds, according to Top Gear.
scenes.caption: 5 CARS AT £625,000 EACH

scenes.text: And the team did not expect to win. Motor Sport says Hazell recalled that not much was done to the car for nineteen ninety-five. The team removed the suspension and engine subframe rubber, added a cage, fitted a rear wing, and raced. The transmission from the road car was the weak link, and Hazell remembered many late nights working on the gearbox.
scenes.caption: THE GEARBOX WAS THE WEAK LINK

scenes.text: Hazell also described why racing looked possible. Motor Sport quotes him saying the team found a friendly series in which no one had really pushed the boat out in terms of preparation and development. So the team believed the car could be made competitive without much work. That belief was tested sooner than anyone expected.
scenes.caption: A FRIENDLY SERIES

scenes.text: And it was quick from the start. Wikipedia's page on the race car says the McLarens took the first three qualifying places at Jerez, and reached two hundred eighty-one kilometers per hour on the Mulsanne straight in practice at Le Mans. Wikipedia's Le Mans page says the cars won six of the seven races of the nineteen ninety-five BPR series up to that point.
scenes.caption: 6 WINS IN 7 RACES BEFORE LE MANS

scenes.text: Hazell said the team knew they could validate a car for four hours, but not twenty-four. So customers paid for a long-distance kit that included a contribution toward a twenty-four-hour test. Motor Sport says that test took place at Magny-Cours, and nine drivers completed it, expecting the car to break.
scenes.caption: A 24-HOUR TEST WITH 9 DRIVERS

scenes.text: Wikipedia's page on the nineteen ninety-five race says the F one GTRs were not expected to win. It says the lighter weight and better downforce of the prototypes were expected to prove superior. And it adds that in April's test, the cars were not on the pace of the Ferraris.
scenes.caption: NOT EXPECTED TO WIN

scenes.text: Then the weather decided. The page describes one of the wettest races in the event's history, with about seventeen hours of steady rain. Wikipedia says the extensive period of rain proved a bigger equalizer and took pressure off the delicate McLaren drivetrains.
scenes.caption: 17 HOURS OF RAIN

scenes.text: Motor Sport says the best McLaren qualifying time, set by J J Lehto, was eleven seconds slower than the pole-winning WR-Peugeot, and eight and a half seconds behind the Courage-Porsche driven by Mario Andretti, Bob Wollek and Eric Hélary. On pure speed, the McLarens were not the fastest cars. But a McLaren led before the end of the first hour.
scenes.caption: ELEVEN SECONDS SLOWER IN QUALIFYING

scenes.text: Motor Sport says John Nielsen led the West-liveried car at the top of each hour from seven in the evening, until clutch problems ended its run shortly before half distance. Wikipedia says Mass and Nielsen had the lead for over eight hours until a broken clutch stopped them at three in the morning. The race was a story of cars falling away.
scenes.caption: THE LEADERS KEPT BREAKING

scenes.text: Later, the two Bells and Wallace fought with Lehto. Motor Sport says Derek Bell regained the lead over Lehto with about four hours left, after Lehto had been lapping about ten seconds faster than anyone else at one point. The page says Wallace praised Bell for stepping up his pace when he had a chance to win.
scenes.caption: BELL v LEHTO IN THE FINAL HOURS

scenes.text: The race had drama on every lap. Motor Sport reports that Derek Bell inadvertently kinked the throttle cable while climbing into the Harrods car, costing two laps. His son Justin Bell came in after one hour when he was supposed to drive two, spooked by the night conditions. He said he had never been so frightened in his life.
scenes.caption: THE BELL FAMILY DRAMA

scenes.text: Andy Wallace drove nearly fourteen hours in that Harrods car. Then the clutch bearing on the release slider failed. The team could not find a replacement, and could not fit a standard clutch. That left the car in direct drive, which caused problems with the gearbox. Wallace said he was using only fifth and sixth gears by the end.
scenes.caption: WALLACE DROVE NEARLY 14 HOURS

scenes.text: Meanwhile, the Japanese-sponsored Kokusai Kaihatsu car, run by Lanzante, moved into the lead in the twenty-second hour. It survived a water pressure alarm that needed a quick stop after the final fuel stop. Lanzante said the strategy was simply to avoid the pits.
scenes.caption: THE LEAD IN HOUR 22

scenes.text: Wikipedia says the winners were J J Lehto, Yannick Dalmas and Masanori Sekiya. Dalmas brought the McLaren home to win by three-quarters of a lap. This was McLaren's first win at Le Mans, at its first attempt. The cars were untested over twenty-four hours, yet they led for all but thirteen laps.
scenes.caption: WON BY THREE-QUARTERS OF A LAP

scenes.text: And the F one GTRs filled four of the first five places. Motor Sport says the Harrods car finished third, two laps behind. GTC Motorsport's best McLaren finished fourth after Ray Bellm crashed in the wet. The Giroix Racing Team car finished fifth after a new starter motor failed early on.
scenes.caption: 4 OF THE FIRST 5 PLACES

scenes.text: Wikipedia also gives a detail about one of the winning drivers. It says Masanori Sekiya had always been passionate about Le Mans, having got married in the town hall during the nineteen eighty-seven race week. Eight years later, he won the race.
scenes.caption: HE MARRIED DURING LE MANS WEEK

scenes.text: The win was not free of controversy. Motor Sport says the winning car was chassis zero zero one R, which had not raced in the global GT series, and was the car used in the Magny-Cours test. McLaren arranged for Lanzante's small team to run it, since McLaren could not run it from the factory.
scenes.caption: CHASSIS 001R

scenes.text: Ray Bellm claimed a contract clause prevented McLaren from running a factory car against privateers. Motor Sport says no such clause existed, and that Bellm had to apologize to Ron Dennis. Lanzante said his squad was the smallest of the GTR teams, with only eight or nine people, and rejected the works allegation.
scenes.caption: A SMALL TEAM, A BIG ARGUMENT

scenes.text: Wikipedia's page on the F one says it was the last road-legal, series-produced sports car to win the twenty-four hours of Le Mans outright. The page says the GTR took first, third, fourth, fifth and thirteenth places in nineteen ninety-five.
scenes.caption: LAST ROAD-LEGAL CAR TO WIN LE MANS

scenes.text: That is thing number two. A road car its creator never wanted to race, built by a team that did not expect to finish, ran in the rain for twenty-four hours and won. And those two things are linked. The same lightness and the same carbon structure that justified gold foil helped the car survive a race that wrecked cars built for it.
scenes.caption: THING TWO: THE ACCIDENTAL CHAMPION

scenes.text: Wikipedia says that in total nine F one GTRs were built for the nineteen ninety-five season, nine more for nineteen ninety-six, and ten for nineteen ninety-seven. Twenty-eight race cars, plus the road cars and special versions. In all, only one hundred six cars were manufactured, the page says.
scenes.caption: ONLY 106 CARS IN TOTAL

scenes.text: On the road, the F one also set a record. Wikipedia says on the thirty-first of March, nineteen ninety-eight, Andy Wallace drove the five-year-old XP five prototype at Volkswagen's test track in Ehra-Lessien. The independently measured two-way average was two hundred forty point one miles per hour.
scenes.caption: 240.1 MPH, MARCH 31, 1998

scenes.text: The peak speed, the page says, was two hundred forty-three miles per hour, measured by McLaren, with the rev limiter raised to eight thousand three hundred r p m. And Gooding and Company notes the F one held the record for the world's fastest production car from nineteen ninety-eight to two thousand five.
scenes.caption: THE WORLD'S FASTEST CAR FOR 7 YEARS

scenes.text: And the road car's price? Top Gear says the new price was five hundred forty thousand pounds, which the Bank of England put at a little over one point one million pounds in two thousand twenty money. Hagerty valued a normal F one at around sixteen million pounds in that article. Gooding and Company reported one sold in twenty twenty-one for twenty point four six five million dollars.
scenes.caption: £540,000 NEW. $20.5 MILLION SOLD

scenes.text: Even the race car's value has soared. Wikipedia lists chassis ten R as sold in twenty twenty-six for a record thirty-four point six five five million dollars. For a car whose factory budget, according to Motor Sport, began with a development budget of seven hundred fifty thousand pounds.
scenes.caption: A GTR SOLD FOR $34.7 MILLION

scenes.text: Both things are connected to one idea. When Murray made the F one, he did not follow a formula. He followed physics. He spent gold on heat and carbon on weight, he put the driver in the middle, and he used a naturally aspirated engine. And the result was a car that did things nobody planned.
scenes.caption: HE FOLLOWED PHYSICS, NOT A FORMULA

scenes.text: The F one's creator himself later said that owning one became uncomfortable. Top Gear quoted Murray saying it became a little untenable to own. He used to drive his car on Sunday mornings, but once it was worth many millions, he was reluctant to risk damaging it.
scenes.caption: "A LITTLE UNTENABLE TO OWN"

scenes.text: So here are the two things again. First, the F one's engine bay was lined with about sixteen grams of gold, and the car came with a gold-plated titanium tool kit. Second, a road car that its designer never meant to race beat purpose-built prototypes at Le Mans, in the rain, on its first try.
scenes.caption: THE TWO THINGS

scenes.text: Which one surprised you more? Tell us in the comments. In the other videos of this series, we compare the McLaren F one with the new McLaren W one, we work out what it really costs to own an F one today, and we tell the story of the man who dreamed it up in an airport.
scenes.caption: WHICH ONE SURPRISED YOU?

scenes.text: And if you want to spend your money on something you can actually drive every day, our twenty twenty-seven Truck Buyer's Guide is linked in the description. Subscribe to Pickup Reality for more stories about the cars and trucks people really talk about.
scenes.caption: SUBSCRIBE: PICKUP REALITY
